BrickMart Retailers, Inc. - Q3 2023 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the BrickMart Retailers, Inc. Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss BrickMart Retailers' results for the Q3. Joining me on today’s call are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Merchandising Officer; Mike Torres, Chief Stores Officer; Emily Grant, Chief Marketing Officer; and Raj Patel, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Alex. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report BrickMart Retailers' performance for the Q3. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Our strongest quarter in over two years was driven by resilient consumer demand in core categories like apparel, home essentials, and footwear, alongside disciplined cost management and accelerating omnichannel execution. Total net sales hit $8.7 billion, up 7.2% year-over-year, beating our guidance and consensus estimates. Comparable store sales rose 5.8%, powered by 3.1% traffic growth and a 2.6% increase in average ticket, outpacing the sector's flat comps. Hardlines grew 9.1%, appliances surged 14.2%, and omnichannel hit 28% of sales with BOPIS at a record 42%. Gross margins expanded 90 basis points to 38.5%, adjusted EBITDA reached $1.1 billion up 12.4%, and diluted EPS was $1.47, up 18%. Free cash flow of $850 million funded $400 million in repurchases. Regionally, Sunbelt markets led with 6.9% comps amid migration trends, while remodels lifted comps 9.2% in upgraded stores. These results validate our stores-first approach, and we've raised full-year guidance to 4.5-5.5% comps, $34.5-35 billion revenue, and $5.60-5.80 EPS.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins to provide more details on our financial results.

Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Johnathan. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q3.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $8.7 billion, a 7.2% increase compared to the same period last year. Gross margin was 38.5%, up 230 basis points year-over-year, primarily driven by favorable product mix, pricing discipline, and supply chain efficiencies. Operating expenses were $3.2 billion, representing 36.8% of revenue. Net income was $450 million, or $1.47 per share. We generated $850 million in cash flow from operations. Inventory levels are currently at $1.28 billion, up 7% year-over-year but optimized at 11.2 weeks of supply.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Before handing over to our merchandising and stores leaders, let me drill deeper into some key operational and financial aspects that underpinned these results, starting with our inventory position, which remains a cornerstone of our operational discipline.

Good afternoon, everyone. As you know, in the brick-and-mortar retail environment—where we're competing head-on with e-commerce giants like Amazon and fast-fashion disruptors like Shein—maintaining optimal inventory levels is critical for preserving gross margins, enhancing cash conversion cycles, and driving comp store sales growth.

Ending inventory for Q3 stood at $1.28 billion, representing a 7% increase year-over-year from $1.20 billion in Q3 2022. On a comparable store basis, excluding the 15 new store openings in high-growth Sun Belt markets, this flattens to a modest 2% YoY uptick. Importantly, this positions us at 11.2 weeks of supply—down 1.2 weeks from 12.4 weeks last year and our best Q3 performance since pre-pandemic levels in 2019. Inventory turns improved to 3.7x for the quarter, up from 3.4x YoY, reflecting stronger SKU velocity across our core apparel, footwear, and home essentials assortments.

Breaking it down by category: Apparel and softlines, 52% of inventory, up 12% YoY to $665 million, driven by robust back-to-school demand and our successful transition to transitional fall merchandise. Sell-through rates hit 68% at full price—our strongest in five years—bolstered by AI-optimized sizing algorithms that reduced stockouts by 22%. We leaned into owned brands like BrickMart Active and Urban Edge, which saw 15% YoY unit growth with 450 basis points of margin expansion, outpacing national brands like Levi's and Nike, where we tightened open-to-buy by 8% to counter softening consumer wallets amid 3.7% CPI inflation.

Footwear, 18% of inventory, flat YoY at $231 million, as we deliberately right-sized after overstocking athleisure last year. We achieved 75% sell-through on key franchises like our exclusive On Cloud collaborations, with inventory turns accelerating to 5.2x—well ahead of peers like Foot Locker's reported 4.1x.

Home goods and hardlines, 25% of inventory, down 5% YoY to $320 million, a proactive de-risking move amid housing market headwinds. Comps here were soft at +1%, but we avoided the markdown carnage seen at peers like Bed Bath & Beyond's remnants or Wayfair's physical store pilots. Small kitchen electrics and seasonal decor drove 85% full-price sell-through.

Other categories, 5%, electronics and impulse items, down 3% YoY to $64 million, focused on high-velocity SKUs with RFID tagging for real-time shrinkage control.

Regionally, in our Northeast cluster—35% of store base—inventories rose 4% YoY but with superior 12.8 weeks of supply, capitalizing on urban density and foot traffic rebound—think Manhattan flagships pulling 18% comps. The Midwest held steady at +1%, buoyed by value-driven traffic in promo-heavy formats akin to Target's Circle ecosystem. We trimmed 3% in the Southeast due to hurricane season uncertainty—stores in Florida and the Carolinas saw cautious replenishment on water-resistant hardlines—while Sun Belt expansions in Texas and Arizona added $45 million in new inventory, aligned with 25% population growth per U.S. Census data.

What enabled this precision? Our technical initiatives are paying off handsomely. We fully rolled out Manhattan Associates' RFID-enabled perpetual inventory system across 85% of our 1,200 stores, slashing cycle counts by 35% and boosting in-stock rates to 96%—critical for buy-online-pickup-in-store, which now fulfills 28% of digital orders. Vendor-managed inventory partnerships with key suppliers like Procter & Gamble and Unilever cover 40% of CPG SKUs, dynamically adjusting based on point-of-sale data and our proprietary demand-sensing AI, which incorporates macroeconomic signals like the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index at 103.0 and regional unemployment trends.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on inventory efficiency as our competitive moat in brick-and-mortar. Post-OmniMax integration—our omnichannel platform—we've shifted 15% of store inventory to serve as micro-fulfillment centers, reducing e-comm delivery times to under 2 hours in 200 metro markets and unlocking $120 million in working capital last year. Forward-looking, we guide to Q4 inventory growth of 4-6% YoY, prioritizing high-margin, low-DIO categories amid holiday build-up. Expect continued DIO compression to 42-44 days enterprise-wide, supporting 200-250 bps of gross margin expansion to 38.5%.

This discipline not only protected our 42% gross margin this quarter—up 110 bps YoY—but also freed up $180 million in cash for share repurchases and CapEx on experiential store remodels, like our 50 'Store of the Future' pilots with AR fitting rooms.

Turning now to sales per square foot, another core productivity indicator. For those less familiar, sales per square foot—or SPSF—measures total net sales divided by our average selling square footage, excluding backrooms and non-revenue areas, underscoring how effectively we're monetizing our physical footprint amid e-commerce pressures.

In Q3, company-wide SPSF came in at $512 per square foot, marking a robust 7.2% year-over-year increase and 3.1% sequential improvement from Q2's $497. This beat our internal guidance of $490-$505 and positions us at the high end of the sector—comparable to a resurgent Macy's or Nordstrom Rack around $500-$550, while broader peers like Kohl's lag at $380-$420.

By segment, apparel—55% of sales—drove upside with $578 SPSF, up 9.4% YoY, fueled by higher conversion rates from AI-optimized planograms increasing fixture turns by 18%. Footwear and accessories at $489, up 5.8%, home goods dipped to $421, down 1.2% due to softer big-ticket traffic amid high interest rates.

Regionally, Northeast urban clusters—New York, Boston, Philly—delivered $645 SPSF, up 12% YoY, from dense foot traffic in high streets like Hudson Yards. Sunbelt markets including Florida and Texas hit $539, up 6.5%, thanks to tourism rebound and 'express' store pilots under 15,000 sq ft yielding 20% higher SPSF. Midwest enclosed malls at $378 flat, weighed by anchor vacancies; Pacific Northwest steady at $501, monitoring Amazon competition.

Drivers include 4.8% comp sales growth from 2.1% traffic lift via BrickMart Rewards with 28 million members and 2.5% average ticket from private-label upselling. Conversion up 110 bps to 28.5%, aided by omnichannel—BOPIS and ship-from-store at 22% of sales. Our 'Store 2.0' remodels, 180 completed, swapped low-yield areas for Nike/Levi's shop-in-shops, boosting localized SPSF 22%. RFID across 40% of chain reduces stockouts 35%; AR try-on kiosks juice cosmetics to $720 SPSF.

Strategically, underperformers below $350 SPSF face 'Optimize or Exit': 25 closures FY24, relos to power centers for 4-6% chain-wide lift. Micro-fulfillment pilots in 10 markets like Walmart's playbook. Q4 guide $525-$540 SPSF, 5-7% YoY.

Next, gross margin details. Our 38.5% gross margin—up 230 basis points from 36.2% last year—marks our strongest expansion in three years, ahead of 150-200 bps guidance. Two-year stacked, up 410 bps, showing durability post-2022 inflation.

Product mix contributed 120 bps: high-margin hardlines like appliances and power tools grew comps 8.2% vs. overall 4.1%, shifting from lower-margin softlines. Private label at 28% of sales, up from 24%, delivers 500-700 bps above national brands—EssentialsPro kitchen appliances from Southeast Asian deals.

Pricing discipline added 80 bps via AI revenue management across 85% of 1,200 stores, optimizing 15,000 SKUs real-time vs. Walmart rollbacks; ASPs up 2.3%, markdowns at 1.8% vs. 2.9%. COGS efficiencies 30 bps: freight to 3.1% from nearshoring 25% imports to Mexico/Vietnam; shrink improved 40 bps to 1.4% via RFID in 150 stores against NRF's $112B industry cost.

Sunbelt at 40.5% up 280 bps on 6.8% comps; Northeast 37.2% up 150 bps weather-hit; Midwest 38.8%. 'Store 2.0' remodels emphasize installed sales at 45%+ margins; SKU rationalization prunes 10% underperformers. Q3 guide 38.7-39.2%, full-year 38.0-38.5%.

On labor costs and store payroll leverage, a standout. Store labor at 17.8% of sales, down 110 bps YoY from 18.9%, best in three years. Absolute payroll up 1.2% to $285M vs. 4.1% comps, 2.9x leverage—$0.34 added per $1 sales.

Sales per labor hour up 7.6% to $142 across 1,250 stores, beating Target's 5%, Costco benchmarks. Hours per store week flat at 2,800 despite 2% traffic.

Drivers: sales productivity from 6% ticket on essentials; pre-planned models keep openings at 4.2% vs. industry 8-10%. AI workforce platform UKG Dimensions across 95% optimizes to 15-min increments with POS/Google Mobility, cuts overtime 18%, under-scheduling 22%—30 bps gain. Self-scanning pilots in 150 stores cut cashier needs 12%.

Wages up 5.8% to $18.42 aligning BLS 6.1%; retention bonuses hold turnover 28% vs. 45%. Southeast stellar 16.2% labor, $155 SPLH; West Coast 20.1% but improved 80 bps. 'Store of the Future' automation, upskilling 15,000 associates lift sales per associate 9%. Q4 60-80 bps improvement.

Marketing and advertising expenses at $152 million, up 12% YoY, 3.1% of sales vs. 2.9%, efficient for 8% top-line. Traditional media 25% or $38M flat; digital 70% up 22% to $106M.

Performance marketing up 28% on Google retail media hyper-local Sun Belt; programmatic $42M 4.2x ROAS via first-party loyalty data, 45M members. Social $32M up 18%, TikTok/Reels viral unboxings generated 2.8M visits; CAC $18 down 15%, LTV up 22%. AI ops on Snowflake/Google tests 500 variants, 25% traffic lift; BrickMart Connect retail media $12M offsetting 8%.

Northeast 10% traffic from SEO; Sun Belt 30% geo-FB; Europe challenged by GDPR. Efficiency ratio 4.8x up from 4.2x. Q3 low-teens growth, 75% digital, scale Connect to $50M, Black Friday blitz.

Shrink/theft pressured margins: rate 1.85% of sales, up 25 bps to $145M loss, 18 bps gross margin hit. Theft 65% of shrink: external 1.20% up 35%, ORC 0.45% up 50%, internal 0.15%, errors 0.05%. Industry $112B per NRF; peers like Target 150 bps hit.

Urban Northeast/West 2.4%, ORC +60% on Dyson/La Mer; rural 1.3%. Self-checkout 42% tender, 25% theft. Response: $250M FY24 invest—AI vision Verkada/Everseen 92% detection, 15% reduction; SKU wraps 65% penetration; Trigo SCO 40% less sweethearting; Risk Engine 88% accuracy, RILA partnerships, RFID CPG.

Expect 15 bps FY24 decline to 1.70%, Q3 1.80%.

Finally, key strategic initiatives update via our "Store Forward" strategy: fleet optimization, omnichannel, supply chain, experiential innovation—adding 150 bps to EPS.

Fleet: 85 remodels up 20%, 12.3% comp lift vs. 8-10% target; shuttered 22 Midwest, opened 15 Express 15k sq ft, $650 SPSF vs. industry $450. H2 120 more remodels.

Omnichannel: BOPIS 28% digital orders up from 22%, app 14.2M users +25%, AI recs 15% conversion; digital 26% sales, logistics 4.2% vs. 5.8%. Curbside-plus CA +32%.

Supply chain: turns 5.2x from 4.1x, Dallas micro-DC; RFID 65% SKUs -22% out-of-stocks; private labels 22% +14%, 45% margins.

Experiential: AR mirrors 200 stores +19% add-to-cart; Green Thread 15% softlines +9% premium; LED/solar 40% fleet -12% utilities.

Aggregate: 4-6% FY24 comps, omni margins +80 bps to 32.5%, $450M FCF, net debt/EBITDA 1.8x.

Now, I'd like to hand it over to Lisa Chen, our Chief Merchandising Officer, to discuss our new product lines, followed by Mike Torres to discuss store operations, Emily Grant to discuss marketing initiatives, and Raj Patel to talk about technology advancements.

Lisa Chen, Chief Merchandising Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. This quarter, we launched our EssentialsPro appliance line, which has seen strong uptake with 14% comp growth and 500 bps margin lift over national brands. We've expanded private labels to 28% penetration, pruning low-velocity SKUs by 10% to focus on high-margin winners like BrickMart Active apparel and Green Thread recycled cotton, driving 68% full-price sell-through. We are excited about the potential of this new product and other upcoming launches in transitional fall and holiday assortments.

Mike Torres, Chief Stores Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. We continue to focus on improving the customer experience in our stores. We have implemented Store 2.0 remodels in 220 locations this year, incorporating open-concept layouts, AR fitting rooms, and dedicated BOPIS zones, delivering 12.3% comp uplifts and $650 per sq ft in express formats. Sales per labor hour hit $142, with lean crews in Sunbelt stores at 16.2% labor costs. Positive results include 5.8% chain-wide comps and 96% in-stock rates.

Emily Grant, Chief Marketing Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Our BrickMart Connect campaign and retail media network have increased brand awareness and driven 25% incremental traffic, with digital at 70% of $152 million spend delivering 4.2x ROAS. Loyalty app push notifications and TikTok virals generated 2.8 million store visits, boosting conversion 15% and tying directly to 28% comps in remodeled stores.

Raj Patel, Chief Technology Officer:
Thank you, Emily. We have invested in AI-driven workforce management, RFID perpetual inventory across 85% stores, and computer vision loss prevention in 1,200 locations, improving inventory turns to 5.2x, reducing shrink 15%, and enabling 2-hour e-comm delivery in 200 markets. Omnichannel tech like dynamic pricing and AR mirrors has enhanced SPLH to $142 and NPS to 78.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Sarah Thompson with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson (Barclays):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of inflation on your sales?

Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer:
Good question, Sarah. Inflation at 3.7% CPI pressured wallets, but we countered with pricing discipline—ASPs up 2.3% via AI optimization—and value-driven private labels growing 14%, holding comps at 5.8%. Essentials like cleaning supplies saw 6% ticket growth, offsetting softer discretionary.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Rossi with Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.

Mike Rossi (Deutsche Bank):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Mike. We're guiding Q4 comps to 4-6%, with tailwinds from holiday builds, remodel momentum at 9.2% uplift, and omnichannel at 28% mix. Risks like weather normalized, but SPSF $525-540 supports it.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Kim with Evercore ISI. Please go ahead.

Lisa Kim (Evercore ISI):
Can you elaborate on the supply chain improvements?

Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer:
Absolutely. Our Dallas micro-fulfillment center and nearshoring 25% imports cut freight to 3.1%, out-of-stocks to 3.2%, turns to 5.2x. VMI with P&G/Unilever and RFID on 65% SKUs enable real-time adjustments tied to POS and macro data.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Patel with Citi. Please go ahead.

David Patel (Citi):
What is the impact from the loyalty program?

Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer:
Our BrickMart Rewards with 28-45 million members drove 2.1% traffic, 22% repeat rate in garden, 60% of sales. Personalized AI recs lifted conversion 15%, BOPIS penetration to 42%, adding 150 bps to margins.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes the question-and-answer session.

Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
